title: From raw temperatures and hourly load to a daily zone table: HDD, CDD, average MW and MWh

explain.prompt: The trader asks: “Why not simply regress load on temperature? And why do you give me both MW and MWh?” Answer in 4–6 sentences with your numbers: what HDD and CDD measure that raw temperature does not (look at the SOUTH zone), and what the difference between average MW and MWh does on 29 October 2023.
rubric: Temperature affects load through two opposite mechanisms: heating below a base temperature, cooling above another. HDD = max(base − T, 0) and CDD = max(T − base, 0) separate them, so each enters a regression linearly.

In the SOUTH zone the two effects cancel in a straight-line fit: corr(load, temperature) is only −0.04, while corr(load, CDD) is 0.53 and corr(load, HDD) 0.26. In NORTH, where heating dominates, temperature alone already gives −0.95.

The base temperature is zone-specific (NORTH 15.5 / 20.0, CENTRAL 16.0 / 22.0, SOUTH 17.0 / 21.0 °C): it encodes the building stock and the use of air conditioning, and a universal base would mismeasure the zones.

Average MW describes the level of demand and is comparable across days; MWh is energy and depends on the number of hours. On 29 Oct 2023 CENTRAL averaged 12,993 MW over 25 hours = 324,813 MWh — about 4 % more energy than the same average on a 24-hour day, purely because of the clock.

The daily temperature is a mean of hourly means on the LOCAL market day, built from UTC observations: averaging the irregular raw observations directly over-weights the extra :20 readings, and a UTC day is shifted by one or two hours from the market day.

Coverage rules make missing data visible: NORTH 14–15 Feb 2023 (station outage, 1 and 10 hours) and SOUTH 5 Mar 2024 (16 of 24 load hours) are left blank instead of averaging what is there; one 99.9 °C sensor code is removed as impossible.
